did.abstract: Civil War-era letters by written by James W. Vanderhoef and addressed to his older sister Mary Ann Guillan in Brooklyn, along with related papers.

acqinfo.head: Immediate Source of Acquisition
acqinfo.p: The collection was purchased by the former Brooklyn Collection but the exact source and date of acquisition are unknown. The collection was formally accessioned in 2020.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: The collection is arranged into four series: Series 1: Pre-Civil War; Series 2: Civil War period; Series 3: Post-Civil War; and Series 4: Other materials.

bioghist.head: Biographical note
bioghist.p: James Wilson Vanderhoef was born around 1837 in New York to Peter S. and Mary Vanderhoef. Peter S. Vanderhoef was born in New Jersey around 1795 and served in the 1st Reg't. (Dodd's) NJ Militia in the War of 1812 in the rank of Private. Peter is listed in the 1850 census and in the Williamsburgh directories as a "carrier" or "Letter carrier." In 1853-4 the family lived at 511 Grand St, moving to 62 Eighth St (Eastern District) by 1856. In one of the final letters dated 1865 Peter is reported as having died. Mary Vanderhoef was also of New Jersey origin. The family also included two daughters: Caroline, born around 1840, and the married sister, Mary Ann (Molly) Guillan, to whom the letters in this collection are addressed.

James entered early upon a military career. Described as 5 ft 7 inches tall, with fair hair, a light complexion and blue eyes, at the age of 16 he enlisted as a musician, joining the N.Y. 1st Artillery Reg't, Co. B, during the War with Mexico.

On 6 Sept. 1861 he re-enlisted for a period of three years "or war" with the 45th Reg't (German Rifles) N.Y.S.V. at the rank of 1st Sergeant. The regiment saw action in several battles, including Cross Keys, 2nd Bull Run, Chancellorsville, and Gettysburg, after which 224 men were reported dead or missing.

On 24 Apr. 1862 Vanderhoef was promoted to 2nd Lieutenant and then again to 1st Lieutenant on Sept 1 of that year. On May 11, 1863 he was promoted to Captain, Co. E. It was at the Battle of Gettysburg on July 1st, 1863 that he was captured and taken prisoner, being held at Libby Prison and other camps. According to the Regimental Descriptive Book, he was returned to his regiment in an exchange on May 13th, 1865.

A note dated 1892 confirms that from June 8, 1863 to June 30, 1865 Vanderhoef held the rank of Captain, after which the position ceased to exist "by reason of the consolidation of the 45 and 58 NY Vols." A report of May 16th 1865, a few days after the exchange, reports him "sick."

Another Register of Enlistments places Vanderhoef back in uniform as of Nov 13, 1866, when he signed up under a Capt. Quimby for a further three years in the regular army. By this time he is 30 and, according to his letters, a married man, having married his "pett" Jennie. Records indicate he may have deserted the army in 1867, and the details of his life thereafter are not known.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The collection consists of 31 letters by written by James W. Vanderhoef and addressed to his older sister, Mary Ann Guillan (born c. 1832) who resided at various addresses in Williamsburg. There is also one letter by another family member (William W. Vanderhoef) of Leipsic, Delaware; three handwritten poems which may or may not be original to the writer; and other documents pertaining to Vanderhoef's imprisonment.

Most of the letters date from the Civil War period and provide an example of the swift promotions possible in times of war. Vanderhoef and the 45th N.Y.S.V. fought in numerous battles, including 1st Bull Run, July 21st 1861, and one letter or journal page written from the battlefield there gives a detailed account of troop movements.
The letters also include many inquiries after family and sometimes obscure discussions of family affairs.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Written from Fort Monroe, VA, these ten letters date from the period of Vanderhoef's first enlistment at the age of 16 as a musician with Co. B, 1st Artillery. Mainly consisting of inquiries after the health of various family members and protestations of eternal friendship, they nevertheless provide moments of interest. He thinks he might have his photograph taken; the soldiers must collect rainwater in barrels, for every well they sink is salty, and he now likes this rainwater "better than Croton water." Fishing for striped bass provides good sport; and in one letter (Dec 20th 1855) Vanderhoef bursts with indignation, having heard that his father is homeless and penniless and no one in the family has taken him in.
The 1854 letters date from July 30 and November 10; the 1855 letters date from March 13, April 7, May 19, November 2, and December 20 and 27; and the 1856 letters date from June 16 and July 31.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Written from various points in the South, these letters provide firsthand information on the movements and activities of the 71st NY Regiment.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: May 1: Describes journey from New York to Annapolis, and writes of the hardships of the 36 hour march to Washington, where the company expected an attack. Various NY regiments are expected momentarily. James is with 30 other boys from Williamsburgh so he is "not a lone." Co H, 71st Regt.
May 10: Says the Regiment was reviewed by the President and Mr Seward last evening. Co. H, 71st Regt.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Apparently written on the battlefield. Gives many details of the engagement.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Lieut Co F 45 Regt N.Y.V.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Long explanation of a misunderstanding which resulted in the Vanderhoef's likeness (photograph) being "smashed to flinders on the sidewalk" by one Jane, whose feelings "must have been offaly hurt."

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Writes that the Union Army has advanced, and he is promoted to 1st Lieutenant. Of Co. "I."

did.unittitle: Camp at Stafford Court House, VA

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Family news and requests. "No ink handy. And not a stamp in camp to be got for love or money."

did.unittitle: Camp near Potomac Creek Station, VA

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: James writes that his company marched around for two weeks until a 15 inch snowfall prevented further movements. Pay is five months overdue.

did.unittitle: Camp at Potomac Creek Station, VA

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: February 9: Brief note. Vanderhoef is in good health and hopes for a furlough.
February 19: Plans a surprise visit to NY.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Plans to be home around March 18th. The following day being Washington's Birthday, a grand review of troops by General Hooker is planned.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The promised visit is put off until March 20.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Wonders why Jennie does not answer his letters.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Such is the demand for his photograph that Vanderhoef has had to send for more copies of it. Writes of the "loss our Regiment had in the seven days fight over the Rappahannock" with detailed description of the battle. 1st Lieut Co "D" 45 Regt NY Vol. Mentions as PS that the Regiment is transferred from 1st brigade 1st Division to 1st Brigade 3rd Division.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: February 14: A letter containing only 6 lines as per prison regulations.
March 27: Writes that he has received only one letter from his sister since December; and hope to be home in April for twenty days. Unfortunately silent on details of life in Libby Prison.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Complains that he has heard nothing of family and friends since April 27th. Has been moved from Charleston to a prison encampment in Columbia with good water supply.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: "Oh wipe away the tear drops from thine eyes…"

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Announces promotion to Capt., Co."E." "It is a good company and I can depend on them in action." Describes 18-month trajectory from Private up the ranks to Captain.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Adams Express Co. New York receipt for one package addressed to Capt. J.W. Vanderhoef, 45 NYV, Libby Prison Richmond.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: War Department notice in reply to enquiry from family, stating that Vanderhoef is "Prisoner of War."

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Letters written by James Vanderhoef after the Civil War.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Announces that he has married Jennie in spite of the disapproval of friends. However the young couple have no money as Vanderhoef is owed $560 by the paymaster. He has been suffering from dysentery, and bemoans his unhappy lot and that of his sister; their father recently died.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Writes that since enlistment he has been so busy making out company papers and looking after things that he has hardly had time to eat or sleep. Passed exam for first Sargeant with no trouble and hope to be put forward for a commission in the regular army. Expects to go to Texas before Dec 20th. Writes that as First Sergeant he is given board, clothing, medical attendance and $24 a month.

did.unittitle: Steamer Rising Star 1,800 miles from New York

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Writes that the ship will be in Aspenwall the next day, and will start for San Francisco in the evening, "a distance of 3,300 miles."

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: This series contains poems, letters, census records, and copies of James Wilson Vanderhoef's military records. These items are undated excepting one 1855 letter.
